title: Time–space separations in polynomial enumeration
formal:
Establish the two separations
\[\mathrm{DelayP}\ne\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}},\qquad\mathrm{IncP}\ne\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}},\]
under a complexity hypothesis, as requested by Open problem 4.1. All four classes retain polynomial-time checkable, polynomial-length solutions. The source does not choose the hypothesis or specify an admissible family of hypotheses. This remains a conditional-lower-bound research direction until that choice is made.
why: The direction concerns whether memory is a separate source of computational power in enumeration once output speed is controlled. It connects practical storage costs of duplicate detection and saturation to structural complexity. Its exact strength depends on the supporting hypothesis, which must be fixed before assessing a precise theorem.
status_note: The source poses a conditional separation program without choosing the hypothesis. The checked WEPA abstract retains this gap, and the July 2026 regularization theorem compares two polynomial-space classes rather than removing the space restriction. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The precise conditional proposition remains unspecified, so the card is pending rather than certified complete or resolved.

sentences: The source asks to separate both polynomial-delay and incremental-polynomial enumeration from their polynomial-space counterparts under a complexity hypothesis.
All target problems retain efficiently checkable, polynomial-length solutions and must enumerate each solution exactly once.
The timing guarantees must hold simultaneously with a memory bound polynomial only in the input size.
Known results either drop polynomial-time verification or compare classes that already both use polynomial space, so they do not settle these separations.
The source does not select the supporting hypothesis, leaving the exact conditional completion target pending.

definitions:
A problem in \(\mathrm{EnumP}\) is a relation \(A(x,y)\) on finite binary strings whose membership is deterministically decidable in polynomial time and whose solution lengths satisfy \(|y|\leq p(|x|)\) for a fixed polynomial \(p\). On input \(x\), enumeration must output every element of the finite set \(A(x)=\{y:A(x,y)\}\) exactly once, produce nothing else, and terminate. No order is prescribed. Let \(n=|x|\) and \(N=|A(x)|\).

The source’s computation model is a deterministic random-access machine with a fixed finite program and integer registers, basic addition, subtraction and multiplication, arithmetic charged by operand bit lengths, and unit-cost register access and other basic instructions. The space cost counts all bits of the working registers and retained output buffers. Emitted output is a write-only stream, not an external readable history. There is no randomness, oracle or advice. Reading or copying an input and preparing an output are included in the time bounds; charging explicitly for polynomially many output bits does not change the classes here.

The class \(\mathrm{DelayP}\) consists of EnumP problems admitting an algorithm and a fixed polynomial \(q\) such that the time before the first output, between each consecutive pair of outputs and between the last output and termination is at most \(q(n)\). If there are no solutions, it terminates within \(q(n)\). The source stops immediately on its final output; charging polynomial terminal work gives the same class by retaining that final result until termination is established. Polynomial preprocessing is included in the initial bound.

The class \(\mathrm{IncP}\) consists of EnumP problems for which some algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) output the first \(k\) solutions within \(C(n+1)^b(k+1)^a\) time, for every input and every \(1\leq k\leq N\), and terminate within the same kind of bound with \(k=N\). Empty outputs require polynomial input time. The exponent may be any fixed integer and does not depend on the input. This is polynomial time in each output prefix, rather than a fixed polynomial delay independent of the number of earlier outputs.

A superscript \(\mathrm{poly}\) requires that the same enumeration algorithm satisfying the timing guarantee also use at most \(s(n)\) working bits at all times, for some fixed polynomial \(s\). In particular, its memory is independent of \(N\) and of the number of solutions already output. Without that superscript, neither class imposes a separate space bound. There are immediate inclusions \(\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\subseteq\mathrm{DelayP}\) and \(\mathrm{IncP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\subseteq\mathrm{IncP}\). The requested inequalities would make both inclusions strict, potentially with different witness relations.

For the background, \(\mathrm P\) denotes languages decidable in uniform deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathrm{NP}\) languages with polynomially verifiable polynomial-length witnesses, \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) languages decidable with polynomial working space and \(\mathrm{EXP}\) languages decidable in time \(2^{n^{O(1)}}\), all on ordinary Turing machines. The later regularization theorem concerns \(\mathrm{IncP}_1^{\mathrm{poly}}\), where the time for \(k\) outputs is bounded by \((k+1)q(n)\). It equates this class with \(\mathrm{DelayP}^{\mathrm{poly}}\); it does not remove a pre-existing superpolynomial storage requirement.
answer_criterion: A precise answer criterion first requires a specified complexity hypothesis, or a noncircular admissibility condition on hypotheses, under which both separations are sought. The source supplies neither. Merely asking for some proposition H that implies the separations is vacuous, since H could be the separations themselves; choosing P different from NP or another standard assumption would add a definite conjecture absent from the source. Once this choice is fixed, a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof must supply, for each desired separation, a polynomially checkable polynomially balanced witness relation with the unrestricted timing algorithm and the claimed impossibility of every simultaneous polynomial-space algorithm. No such additional hypothesis is selected here.

source_formulation.text: Prove that DelayP and IncP differ from their polynomial-space counterparts, assuming a complexity hypothesis.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open problem 4.1; the source leaves the supporting complexity hypothesis unspecified.

context_blocks.text: Fast enumeration may accumulate a large history of answers, use it to generate new answers or buffer irregular output. The question asks whether this memory can be essential to the existence of a good timing guarantee. The memory consumption of one familiar algorithm is not evidence that every algorithm for its relation needs that much space.

Every EnumP relation can be enumerated in polynomial space by scanning all possible bounded-length witnesses and checking each. That procedure need not have polynomial delay or incremental polynomial time. The unknown issue is the simultaneous use of small space and the requested timing guarantee, not polynomial-space enumerability by itself.

If P = NP, prefix-existence tests for any EnumP relation become polynomial-time decidable. Depth-first search over candidate witness prefixes then enumerates solutions with polynomial delay and polynomial space. Thus all four classes collapse to EnumP under that hypothesis, and a separation would entail P different from NP. The converse implication is not supplied by the source.

Dropping polynomial-time solution verification changes the problem. The source can hide the answer to an exponential-time decision problem among exponentially many trivial outputs; a polynomial-space enumerator would reveal that answer in polynomial space. This gives a conditional separation under EXP different from PSPACE for the larger framework. Its special output cannot generally be checked in polynomial time, so it is not a witness for the EnumP-restricted target.

The July 2026 regularization theorem proves equality between polynomial-space linear incremental enumeration and polynomial-space polynomial-delay enumeration. Both sides already obey the same space restriction. It therefore does not prove equality, or strict inequality, between unrestricted-space and polynomial-space classes in this card.

Restricted black-box lower bounds measure algorithms that can access only a supplied generator, sometimes with an output-order constraint. The requested class separations permit arbitrary algorithms reading the relation’s original input and freely choosing the output order. The stronger restrictions in a black-box lower bound cannot silently be imported into this target.

The later WEPA abstract continues to ask for conditional separations at fixed incremental exponents without selecting a hypothesis. Neither that formulation nor the known regularization theorem resolves the missing choice in the historical request. Selecting a standard assumption, or instead asking for an unconditional two-class separation, would be an explicit change of target.

statement_review.remaining_issue: Open problem 4.1 asks for both space separations assuming some complexity hypothesis, but specifies neither the hypothesis nor a noncircular admissible class of hypotheses. An existential H implying the target can be satisfied tautologically by H equal to the target. The EXP-versus-PSPACE result drops polynomial-time verification and does not supply this missing choice for EnumP.
